utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the cases.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is the Case Number IT-04-74-I, The Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And may I first ask to all six accused whether they can hear me in a language they understand. Could I perhaps first hear from Mr. Prlic whether he can hear me in a language he understands. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you. I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prlic. Then Mr. Stojic. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I could hear in a language I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same question for Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] I can hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same question for Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then finally, you, Mr. Pusic, can you also hear me in a language you understand. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] I could hear and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. By addressing you all, I take it that you also confirmed your identity, that you are Mr. Prlic, you are Mr. Stojic, you are Mr. Praljak, you are Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Coric, and Mr. Pusic. Then I would like to have the appearances. We have already heard from the accused. Could, perhaps, first counsel present themselves, first counsel for Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SALAHOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm attorney-at-law, Camil Salahovic from Zagreb representing Mr. Jadranko Prlic. Next to me is my esteemed colleague, Zelimir Par.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salahovic. Mr. Stojic is assisted by?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney-at-law, Defence counsel from Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, representing Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I invite counsel for Mr. Praljak to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Kresimir Krsnik, I'm an attorney-at-law from Zagreb, Republic of Croatia. I will be lead counsel for Mr. Slobodan Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krsnik. Then could counsel for Mr. Petkovic present herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good afternoon. I'm attorney-at-law Vesna Alaburic. My head office is in Zagreb, Croatia. I will be defending General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- Mr. Coric is assisted by?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Tomislav Jonjic, attorney-at-law from Zagreb, Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Jonjic. And then finally, I would like to invite counsel for Mr. Pusic to introduce himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Marinko Skobic, attorney-at-law from Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will be representing Mr. Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skobic. May I have the appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. May it please the Court, appearing on behalf of the Prosecutor, Kenneth Scott, senior trial attorney. With me today are trial attorneys Pieter Kruger, Garlone Egels, Miguel Longone, and our case manager Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. Then the only anonymous person at this moment is myself. My name is Judge Orie. I am a Judge in Trial Chamber I. The cases against all six of you have been assigned to Trial Chamber I, consisting of Judge Liu, Judge El Mahdi and myself. And Judge Liu has assigned me as Pre-Trial Judge. These decisions have been taken yesterday. I don't know whether the Defence counsel have received already copies of it, but they are available for them. Could I first ask the assistance of -- I have a zoom in my... This is better. So now I don't hear anything at all. I'm just testing. I'm testing my earphones. All yours are functioning, but mine is still not. I am trying to -- is it channel 4? I don't hear anything on channel 4. I apologise for the delay, but I have some additional noise in my earphones. But that shouldn't be a major problem. Having introduced myself, I'd like to explain to you what the purpose of this initial appearance is. Article 20, paragraph 3 of the Statute informs us that I should read the indictment to you, that I should satisfy myself that your rights are respected, and that would specifically mean at this moment that you're informed about the charges that have been brought against you, that your right to be assisted by counsel is respected. Then, I have to satisfy myself that you understand the indictment, and I should instruct you to enter a plea. That means that you enter a plea of guilty or not guilty. Since you arrived only yesterday in The Hague, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence give you an opportunity to enter a plea within the next 30 days. But if you want to enter a plea today, you are allowed to do so. So I'll move to the first part of Article 20 of the Statute. And I have to satisfy myself that you're assisted by counsel. And now I address counsel. I was informed that you're not assigned by the Registrar, but you're all counsel of choice by the accused. Do I have to understand this choice as being a choice on a more permanent basis, or is it mainly for this initial appearance that you'll assist your accused? Could I hear that from each counsel, perhaps first Mr. Salahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can answer on behalf of my colleague, Mr. Salahovic and myself. Our client authorised us to represent him on a permanent basis. We know that there is no authorisation that is full guarantee that we'll remain until the end, and we don't know the stance of the Registry for the time being concerning our engagement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. What I can say is that it was the will of my client that I should represent him as his Defence counsel, and that implies a permanent basis and the trust that my client has in me. And in keeping with the letter and spirit of the Statute and the Rules of Procedure prevailing in this lofty court, I think there should be no problem because the underlying intent is to protect the fundamental rights of the client, including his right to a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Olujic, did you discuss with your client that you are assisting at this moment Mr. Rajic who is accused before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Even before I undertook the Defence of Mr. Bruno Stojic, I discussed with my other client, Mr. Ivica Rajic, who is currently involved in proceedings before this Tribunal. And he unconditionally accepted that I should also defend Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there no conflicting interests between your two client, Mr. Olujic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it true that the indictment against Mr. Rajic very much focuses on the Vares municipality, and that the Vares Municipality and what happened here also appears in the present indictment against Mr. Stojic in paragraph 204 and following?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. The indictment against Mr. Bruno Stojic refers to Stupni Do inter alia. However, when we read the indictment and take into account the scope by which Mr. Bruno Stojic is encompassed in the view of the Prosecution and the role that my client had, we see no points of contact and no reason for any conflicting interests between these two clients, Mr. Ivica Rajic and Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Stojic is held responsible for acts for which Mr. Rajic is charged as a perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, yes, because that is the way the indictment is worded. But the very position in the hierarchy that my client held had no points of contact with Mr. Ivica Rajic. Mr. Stojic was never in a position to command any troops of police forces, army, or other forces; whereas Mr. Rajic is a military officer of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I understand from the indictment, Mr. Stojic is held responsible not only for nonmilitary, but also for what happened militarily on the ground. Let's not pursue this matter in full detail at this very moment, although the question of whether a direct command contact is the criterion to be applied is unclear to me at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. very moment. I heard your submission in that respect. Let me ask you, Mr. Stojic. I take it that you were aware of Mr. Olujic also defending Mr. Rajic who is charged with the events, especially in the Vares Municipality for which you are charged as well. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I insist on being defended by Mr. Zeljko Olujic. He was my choice, and I will be as emphatic on keeping him as my counsel as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I do understand that for this very moment where there is nothing more asked from you to enter a plea, a plea which -- I don't know what it will be, but it can always be -- if it will be a not guilty plea, it can always be changed. Of course, the other way around would be more difficult. You can't plead guilty now and then plead not guilty tomorrow. I ask you to keep that clearly in mind. And when you say you insist on being defended by Mr. Olujic, I have to inform you that Defence counsel are bound by the regulations established by this Tribunal, and that it depends on those regulations whether your wish, if I may interpret it that way, finally can become true. But I do understand that you're fully aware of the present situation of Defence counsel defending two accused involved in charges regarding the same events, but from a very different position. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] I can only repeat that I insist on being defended by Mr. Zeljko Olujic. I have discussed with him over the last four or five days, and we touched upon this subject as well. And still, I insist on having him as my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it's your specific wish to be defended by Mr. Olujic. Then for the -- Mr. Prlic, you are aware that Mr. Par has defended Mr. Martinovic before this Tribunal? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am informed about that. I have discussed this with my counsel, Mr. Par. He said that the matter will be resolved following due procedure with the competent authorities of this Tribunal, primarily the OTP, and I believe any conflict of interest will be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Praljak, you are aware that your Defence counsel, Mr. Krsnik, has previously presented Mr. Naletelic in this Tribunal? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I am aware of the fact, Your Honour. And if there is no obstacle in the Rules of this Tribunal, I have already testified before esteemed Mr. Scott here, and I wish to say that if there is no obstacle in the Rules, then I would like to keep Mr. Krsnik as my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From the fact that I did not ask any specific questions, you could conclude that at this moment no specific circumstances came into my mind that might indicate that there could be a conflict of interest. Then finally, I have Mr. Par. Mr. Krsnik, if you would like to make observations in this respect. I've no specific questions. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I should say just a few words. Before I got involved in the Defence of Mr. Prlic, I had discussions with Vinko Martinovic, my client, and received his repeated consent to my engagement as Defence counsel for Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no particular comment considering that Mr. Scott and I have spent in this courtroom almost three years. I don't want to take any more of your time. I have no particular comments, and I believe there is no conflict of interest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Coric, a similar question in respect of you. You are aware that your Defence counsel, Mr. Jonjic, defends at this moment Mr. Ljubicic before this Tribunal. Mr. Ljubicic, who is charged with crimes that allegedly were committed in the same period, but not in the villages and municipalities, but I could not just by reading the indictment exclude any relevant overlap in, for example, command structures. You are aware of the fact that Mr. Jonjic represents Mr. Ljubicic? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm aware that Mr. Jonjic is defending Mr. Ljubicic. We believe there is no conflict of interest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jonjic, is there any submission you'd like to make here? I have no specific questions, apart from the observations I just made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is useful just to mention that Mr. Ljubicic was informed in due time of the possibility that I would appear as lead counsel for Mr. Coric, and he gave his full consent. And in few of the fact that you emphasised, namely, that events for Mr. Ljubicic is charged are not covered by this indictment, we believe there is no conflict of interest. However, it is up to the Registry -- or the Tribunal, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jonjic. I just want to make quite clear to both you, counsel, and accused that from the mere fact that we will now continue, that you could not conclude that there's a final determination by the Chamber or by me as a Pre-Trial Judge that conflicting interest that would prevent you from acting on behalf of one of these accused are absent. It is a question which, specifically in respect of counsel and accused I just addressed, is still open. There's no final determination on that. Then may I ask each of you whether you have read and discussed the indictment brought against you with counsel. Mr. Prlic, did you? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have. I understand why I am charged by the indictment, although I did not understand the underlying charges. If it is necessary to say it in so many words for the record, I am saying now that I have received and understood the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And same question for you, Mr. Stojic, whether you received and you have read and discussed with counsel -- these are three questions, whether you received it, whether you read it, and whether you discussed it, the indictment? THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] I have received the indictment. I have read it and discussed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Praljak, same question for you, or same three questions for you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have received the indictment, Your Honour. I have discussed the indictment with my Defence counsel. And on a logical level, I understood the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also read it? Yes. When I ask you whether you read it, it is presumed that you received the indictment in your own language. If that's not the case, please inform me. Then, Mr. Petkovic, for you also the three questions, whether you received it, whether you read it, and whether you discussed it with counsel. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have received the indictment. I've read the indictment. I have received a copy in my own language in as far as it could be in my own language, and I have discussed the indictment with my Defence counsel. I understand what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Coric, same three questions for you. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've received the indictment. I've read the indictment. And I've discussed the indictment with my Defence counsel. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Coric. And finally, Mr. Pusic. You're always the last, but same three questions for you. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I have understood the indictment. I've received the indictment. And I have discussed the indictment with my Defence counsel. There are a lot of things I didn't quite understand in view of the fact that I was involved in humanitarian issues during the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the lack of understanding was not caused by the language of the indictment, but rather on that you could not understand how you could be charged as you were charged? THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] I understood the language of the indictment, but there was still quite a number of things of which I stand indicted that I failed to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do you fail to understand what you're charged with, or do you fail to understand why someone could decide that it would be fair to charge you with these counts or these facts? THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] As I was involved in humanitarian work, there are quite a number of things that I hear now for the first time. I was never physically present there. That is why I was surprised to find myself indicted of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I better understand what your nonunderstanding actually means. If you would prefer to remain seated, then I will not feel in whatever way offended by it. So if that would be more comfortable for you, please remain seated if -- as you wish. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have all read the indictments; and unless one of the counsel would disagree that he discussed it with his accused, his or her accused, I take it that the indictments were discussed with them. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There's, however, one issue which is not entirely clear to me. Did you receive, and I'm now addressing counsel, did you receive any of the annexes to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Jadranko Prlic Defence has received all the annexes and attachments to the indictment; some of them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that true for -- could we do another way. If one -- if counsel did not receive the annexes, I would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need for me to speak then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a question for the accused: Did you read also the annexes to the indictment, and were you able to discuss them with counsel? If any of you had no opportunity to read or discuss it, I'd like to know. Perhaps first Mr. Prlic, if you... THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't understand what "annex" means. Is this to do with technical issues in relation to the law? In that case, yes, I have received those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it has got nothing with the law. As a matter of fact, attached to the indictment, one single indictment against all of you, in annexes the identity of the victims, whether killed or wounded or sexually abused, is given in relation to the locations where the crimes allegedly had occurred. And further details are given in respect of sniping incidents in Mostar. I see some confusion. Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said before that we have received all these annexes, without even knowing that there were any such documents to be attached to the indictment. When I said that we had everything, what I had in mind were the usual technical attachments to an indictment, the kind that we usually have. What you're telling us now, I can only say that our Defence has not received any such documents. I don't know about the other Defence teams, but probably my colleagues would have informed me of receiving any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, first of all, when my client received the indictment, there were no attachments, no annexes, just the text of the indictment itself in both Croatian and English. Having arrived in The Hague, more specifically today at 1400 hours, we received some of the documents, documents of procedural nature. The arrest order and so on and so forth, I do not want to go now into enumerating all the documents that I've looked at half an hour ago. But what you have just told us about, Your Honour, we have so far not received any of those. I'm not sure about the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you didn't receive it, although it appears from the indictment itself that there should be annexes. For example, if I draw your attention to paragraph 106, you'll see that reference is made to "annex." I also can understand why you didn't receive it, because they are still under seal and confidential. I did, however, understand, Mr. Scott, that the Prosecution would not insist on keeping them under seal, but that they should remain confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please Court, Your Honour, you're absolutely correct. As you just indicated, the indictment on its face indicates that there are annexes, confidential annexes, attached as part of the indictment. The situation that we confronted was that there was certain information that was very sensitive, identifies particular victims and potential witnesses by name. And until such time as the accused could be brought before the custody of the Tribunal and such protective measures ordered by this Chamber, we were not in a position to be able to make that information available to the accused. This was all previously addressed with Judge Antonetti, and as you pointed out just now, Your Honour, the annexes themselves remained sealed. Further, as Your Honour just correctly stated, the Prosecution has no interest whatsoever in keeping that information from the accused. In fact, it's prepared to provide that information today, provided that protective measures are entered and the Prosecution would be satisfied if Your Honour could make oral rulings or orders to make it very clear to the accused that the annexes will be provided in the strictest of confidence, not to be disclosed for any purpose at all to any other person other than the immediate Defence teams, unless and until -- until other Court orders might be entered. If Your Honour is prepared to do that, and we could proceed that way if you wish, we're in the Chamber's hands, we'd be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we continue, I would like to have an explanation, please. These annexes, what exactly do they mean? Are they part of the indictment, an integral? Are they an integral part of the indictment or something outside of the indictment itself? If those annexes are part of the indictment, if they are considered part of the indictment, in that case I'm afraid I must say that our clients have not had a proper chance to look at the indictment. I hope the Chamber can assist me with this. Just another thing briefly. In the indictment itself, there's a reference to a number of annexes. This was supposed to be some kind of warning to the Defence that there were more documents to be had. We do not believe that the Defence should be put in a position to beg the Prosecutor for more documents concerning the indictment itself. The fact that there were annexes means nothing to us before we've had a chance to look at those and be in possession of those documents. In relation to the proposals made by Mr. Scott, I have to say that as an attorney-at-law I simply do not understand whether these annexes are part of the indictment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give an opportunity for another counsel to address the matter, perhaps I should give you a little bit more information. The lifting of the confidentiality by Judge Antonetti did not include the annexes. Let me first of all explain to you exactly what these annexes are. These annex -- it's one annex, several parts. In this annex, details are given about the identity of persons killed, wounded, or sexually abused related to the various locations. So you'll find there, in this location, the two people killed, names are X, Y. And then in the annex also some additional details are given in respect of the sniping incidents that took place in Mostar. That means, name of the person involved and where it happened and what kind of weapon was used. I see that you're standing, Mr. Pusic. Is there any specific reason, or is it just to overcome some discomfort being seated. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I have some health problems. As you can see, I'm on crutches. I can't sit down, and I can't stand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're not able to follow these proceedings being present here, I'd like to hear either from you or from counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may explain briefly, my client had undergone a very complicated spine surgery last week. At his own risk, he left the hospital despite being cautioned by the doctors not to leave. He responded to your call to receive the indictment. And in view of the medical recommendations he received, he shall be able to follow the proceedings here, be seated for perhaps 15 or 20 minutes at a time. But after, that he has to stand up to relax a bit because that's what his spine -- the condition of his spine requires. Therefore, I would ask your permission for my client to stand up occasionally from time to time for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic, just take the position which is more comfortable to you, although I do understand that all positions are uncomfortable. But take the best one. And whenever you feel that you'll not be able to follow these proceedings here because of your medical condition, please inform me. Then, I'll return to where we were, and that's the annexes. I said that a piece of information is also contained in this annex relating to details of specific sniping incidents in Mostar, sniping incidents which you find - let me just check - I think in -- well, it's somewhere in 24, 25, or 26 of the indictment, that specifically the sniping incidents are mentioned. And you'll find further details about these incidents. Of course, I've given it some thought prior to this hearing whether we could proceed. And apart from that, I'd like to hear from you whether, without having seen this, or if you'd prefer to have a short break to read it, if I would have given an order that the seal is lifted. I came to the conclusion that it very much depends on what the accused intend to plea. Since if you enter a plea of not guilty because you say that the -- you are no member of the joint criminal enterprise, the joint criminal enterprise had not these purposes, did not even exist, people were not killed, then, of course it might not be of major importance to know exactly whether Mr. X or Mrs. Y or Child Z was not killed, if you deny the killing at all or if you deny responsibility for the joint criminal enterprise or another form of participation in that killing. So therefore, the absence of knowledge, of course, gains great importance if there's any intention to enter a guilty plea. It might have less importance if there is an intention to plead not guilty. On the other hand, I'm willing, having heard the observation of the Prosecution, I'm willing to just take a break for 10 minutes, after having given an oral ruling, after you have been provided -- I don't know, in all languages, Mr. Scott? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They can be provided in both English and in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S. So I'd now like to hear from you what you'd like to do, to say no, with the lack of knowledge of these annexes, we could not proceed today. Then fine, we'll stop. We'll give a ruling on whether the annexes will be provided to you, or whether you say we would like to proceed but not until we have had an opportunity for 10 minutes at least to get an impression of what's in those annexes, in that annex, or that you say since our clients intend to enter a plea of not guilty, it's of no major importance anyhow to know what details there are on events that we deny to have taken place at all. Could I please hear first from Mr. Par or Mr. Salahovic. Or if you want to confer first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we cannot take this decision without first conferring with our client. Therefore, my proposal is let us have a short break to consult our clients and the other Defence teams to look at the documents, and then come back to the courtroom to give you our final position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this a position shared by all Defence counsel? I see nodding, apart from you, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. I agree as well. By way of introduction, I wanted to say that I do not oppose the idea of a break now. But what seems to be beyond doubt on the part of the Prosecution, and thank you too, Your Honour, for the clarification you have provided. It has not been challenged that these annexes had a part of the indictment, an integral part of the indictment, and therefore I would like to have 10 minutes to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, my client is seeking permission to address you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have had discussion among ourselves. I believe our plea will be the same for everyone: Not guilty. If I understand Mr. Scott correctly, there's a possibility to inspect these annexes. And then the Prosecution opposes the request for provisional release. If that is indeed the case, even before we've had a look at the documents, we would like to have at least 10 or 15 minutes, a break, to confer with each other and to see what we do next. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, provisional release is not an issue that has been raised until now. So what I suggest I didn't very moment, but I'm also looking at security, whether it would be possible that counsel confer briefly with their clients in the courtroom during a short break. I would say 5 to 10 minutes would be enough to just read the annexes, or at least get a first impression, and then confer with your clients. May I ask... But before having a break, of course, I should give an oral order. The oral order I give at this moment is that the annex to the indictment will be unsealed, but remains confidential. That means that Defence counsel and accused are not allowed to communicate with anyone outside your Defence team - I don't know whether you have already given a list of the members of your Defence team to the Registry. If not, then it means that it's only you, that means seven counsel and six accused, who have access to this document that will be provided to you after this order by the Prosecution. We'll then have a short break of -- until a quarter past 3.00 and see how we will proceed. We'll have a break for 10 minutes. --- Break taken at 3.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the annex has been disclosed to Defence counsel and accused. Is there a unanimous answer on the question whether we could proceed today or whether you need more time to prepare with the accused what plea to enter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can proceed. I think that's a unanimous position on the part of all the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Par. I always take it if one of the counsel speak on behalf of all of them, I expect a firm protest whenever you say something you would not agree with. Then we'll proceed, but not after having clarified the following issue also to the accused: Whenever I speak during this hearing about an incident or a crime or a victim, you should always understand that as the crime allegedly committed, or the incident that allegedly took place, or an alleged victim, because at the very start of these proceedings, nothing has yet been established, and you are presumed innocent until proven guilty. Although it is not very practical to add to every word I say "alleged" or "allegedly," that would keep us for another hour in this courtroom. So therefore -- but that's the way you should understand my words when I'm referring to crimes or victims or incidents or whatever. Then I am supposed to read the indictment to you. Since you all know now that the indictment contains 60 pages, I'd like to know whether you want me to read it in its entirety or whether I should give a summary. At the end of the summary, I'll read each of the counts to you. And if you'd like to enter a plea today, you can plead guilty or not guilty to that count. So there are two questions. First, whether the indictment should be read in its entirety; and the second question is whether the accused, and that could be different for any of them, want to enter a plea today. Could I hear, to start with, with one answer. Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of our Defence team is that there is no need to read the entire indictment. We would like to have the summary read as briefly as possible in order to expedite today's proceedings. And the other question was -- I forget. We are prepared to enter a plea today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'll try to keep the summary, then, short. But you should also understand that this is not a kind of a private meeting between two parties and the Judge, but this is a public hearing in which it should be clear not only for those participating in this hearing, but also for those attending this hearing what it is all about. The indictment brought against you consists of seven parts. In the first part, the identity is -- of all of the accused is given, and it is described what positions you have held during the periods of the indictment. In the second part of the indictment, a joint criminal enterprise is described and the way in which you, the accused, allegedly took part in that joint criminal enterprise. In part 3 of the indictment, an overall view is taken on the general, political, and military context in which the crimes were committed and describes in broader terms how the joint criminal enterprise operated in it and what kind of activity you have developed in this political and military context. Part 4 of the indictment describes in more detail what happened in more than ten locations, such as municipalities or detention centres or military prisons, and mentions exactly what crimes specifically were committed in each of these locations. Then in part 5, the indictment confronts you with the basis of your criminal responsibility in a variety of alternatives, under Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. And although participation in a joint criminal enterprise may be given much attention here, including for the possibility that you aided and abetted in the joint criminal enterprise, apart from having participated in it, this does not exclude in the view of the Office of the Prosecution your responsibility for planning, instigating, ordering or committing, or aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of these specific crimes. Each of you is, therefore, also charged as a coperpetrator and/or an indirect perpetrator of these crimes apart from your responsibility as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. Further, your responsibility is described in terms of your participation or involvement in a system of ill-treatment. And reference in this respect is specifically made to a network of concentration camps and detention facilities, and the systematic deportation of Bosnian Muslims and various forms of physical and sexual abuse which took place in that system. And in this respect, I'd like to ask a short question to you, Mr. Scott: Is this system of ill-treatment a separate and additional form of responsibility under Article 7(1), or is it just an explanation of one of the other forms?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, the position of the Office of the Prosecutor, Your Honour, is that this might be what's sometimes called the second variation of a joint criminal enterprise. There are sometimes, and I hate to use colloquialisms on this, but we sometimes talk in joint criminal enterprise one, two, and three. And there is a second version involving systems of ill-treatment. And the Prosecution views this as a distinct, related but distinct, theory of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it, but I just wanted to be sure that this was a correct way of understanding the indictment. Finally, the indictment holds you responsible in your capacity as a superior or as a commander, exercising de jure or de facto and/or de facto control as a superior official or an officer. This charge includes that you failed to do whatever you could have done to prevent the crimes to be committed by those under your supervision or under your command, and that you failed to punish, remove, or discipline those who committed those crimes. I now move to the sixth part of the indictment. In the sixth part Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the indictment, 26 counts are listed mentioning the crimes you are charged with. In this part of the indictment, reference is made to the applicable legal provisions and also to the paragraphs in the indictment where you find the facts underlying these description legal terms of the crimes. Then in the seventh part of the indictment you find additional allegations of the indictment, setting out some general elements relevant in relation to some or sometimes all of the crimes charged, such the characteristics of the armed conflict or of the widespread and systematic attack in which the crimes allegedly were committed, special intent in respect of some crimes, or a description of the parties and individuals involved in view of their status under treaty law. I don't have to draw your attention again to the confidential, as it reads in my note, but not -- well, still confidential, but not under seal any more, the annex to the indictment in which details are given about the identity of persons killed, wounded, sexually abused in the various locations and under various circumstances, and about -- details about sniping incidents against civilians in Mostar. This is a general overview. I will summarise or quote some parts of the indictment which seem to be of even greater importance than others. And I'll do that in somewhat more detail. First of all, I'll give you the list of crimes in, as I said, part 6 of the indictment which clarifies what crimes you're charged with. That is persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds as a crime against humanity; murder as a crime against humanity; willful killing as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; rape as a crime against humanity; inhuman treatment through sexual assault, also a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; deportation as a crime against humanity; unlawful deportation of a civilian as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; inhumane acts by forcible transfer, a crime against humanity; unlawful transfer of a civilian, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; imprisonment as a crime against humanity; unlawful confinement of a civilian as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; inhumane acts through the conditions of confinement, also a crime against humanity; inhuman treatment through the conditions of confinement as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; cruel treatment also related to conditions of confinement as a violation of the laws and customs of war; inhumane acts as a crime against humanity; inhuman treatment as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; cruel treatment as a war crime; unlawful labour, a war crime; extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity as a war crime; destruction or willful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion or education as a war crime; appropriation of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; plunder of public or private property as a war crime; unlawful attack on civilians as a violation of the laws and customs of war, that is a war crime; unlawful infliction of terror on civilians, specifically related, as the previous count, to Mostar; and cruel treatment related to the Mostar siege as a war crime. I've got one question in this respect, Mr. Scott: When I read these crimes, under count 25, reference is made to Article 3 under (d) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Could you explain what 3(d) means in terms of unlawful infliction of terror on civilians because under 3(d) I read not -- it says seizure of -- destruction or willful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion, charity, and education, the arts and sciences, historic monuments, and works of art and science. I, without further explanation, I have some difficulties in reconciling the unlawful infliction of terror on civilians with Article 3(d).

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think -- Your Honour, I think in looking at that it, might have been more accurate to simply refer to Article 3 for purposes of unlawful infliction of terror because unlawful infliction of terror under the violations of the laws or customs of war I think encompasses, in fact, one, quite arguably, all subcategories (a) through (e). That would be my initial answer, Your Honour, to that. I would have to probably to give a full answer, to fairly -- to be completely transparent, Your Honour, I would need to consult probably and look at it closer and talk with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you find an opportunity to do so. For the time being, if this would confuse you, I would like to hear from you, but it might be that by mistake the Prosecution included a letter (d) where it just wanted to refer to Article 3 of the Statute. Article 3, which in general terms, have been used in earlier indictments before this Tribunal in relation to the unlawful infliction of terror on civilians. Having gone through the crimes for which you are held responsible, I would further give some details in respect of the joint criminal enterprise on which the indictment is focussing. It's not excluding other bases for your responsibility, but it's very much focussing on the joint criminal enterprise. I'd like to read to you what is the aim of this joint criminal enterprise as it is given in paragraph 15 of the indictment. It says that the aim was to politically and militarily subjugate, permanently remove, and ethnically cleanse Bosnian Muslims and other non-Croats who lived in areas on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were claimed to be part of the Croatian community, and later Republic, of Herceg-Bosna, and to join these areas as parts of a Greater Croatia, whether in the short term or over time, and whether as part of the Republic of Croatia or in close association with it. By force, fear, or threat of force, persecution, imprisonment, and detention, forcible transfer and deportation, appropriation and destruction of property and other means which constituted or involved the commission of crimes which are punishable under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Tribunal Statute. The territorial ambition of the joint criminal enterprise was to establish a Croatian territory with the borders of the Croatian Banovina, a territorial entity that existed from 1939 to 1941. It was part of the joint criminal enterprise to engineer the political and ethnic map of these areas so it would be Croat dominated both politically and demographically. This is how the purpose or the aim of the joint criminal enterprise is described in the Tribunal. It's also described that the joint criminal enterprise did exist of more persons than just you. Apart from you, the indictment mentions by name, apart from many others who are not mentioned by name, Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Janko Bobetko, and Mate Boban as participants in this joint criminal enterprise, all of those persons mentioned by name have deceased. In paragraph 17 of the indictment, it is described by what means you allegedly participated as leaders in this joint criminal enterprise. Without reading it all, I'll give important parts to you. By establishing, organising, directing, funding, facilitating, supporting, maintaining, and/or operating Herceg-Bosna/HVO governmental and political structures and processes (or various elements thereof); by establishing, organising, commanding, ordering, directing, funding, facilitating, participating in, supporting, maintaining, and/or operating the Herceg-Bosna/HVO military, police, intelligence, and other forces; by initiating, promoting, planning, preparing, participating in, supporting, and/or encouraging the development, formulation, dissemination, and/or implementation of Herceg-Bosna/HVO political, governmental, and/or military policies, programmes, plans, decrees, decisions, regulations, strategy or tactics which were used as bases or vehicles for various actions against or to the disadvantage of Bosnian Muslims; by instigating, supporting, encouraging, facilitating, and/or participating in the dissemination of information and propaganda to Bosnian Croats, it was intended to advance the joint criminal enterprise. It's alleged that you did it by planning, instigating, commanding, directing, participating in, facilitating or supporting the HVO takeover of various municipal governments and efforts to "Croatise" the Bosnian Muslim and other non-Croat population in areas which the Herceg-Bosna/HVO leaders claimed were part of Herceg-Bosna; by encouraging, controlling, funding, facilitating, assisting, and/or participating in the production, acquisition, or distribution of military equipment, arms, ammunition, funds, logistical support, and other means which were used to advance the joint criminal enterprise; by requesting, obtaining, arranging, facilitating, and/or coordinating the participation and assistance of elements of the Republic of Croatia government, armed forces, police, and intelligence services; by establishing, organising, directing, funding, facilitating, supporting, participating in, maintaining, and/or operating a system of Herceg-Bosna/HVO prisons, concentration camps, and other detention facilities; by establishing, organising, directing, funding, facilitating, supporting, participating in, maintaining, and/or operating a system for the deportation or forcible transfer of Bosnian Muslims to other countries or to parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were not claimed or controlled by Herceg-Bosna as part of and in furtherance of the joint criminal enterprise; by ordering, instigating, promoting, encouraging, facilitating, and/or implementing the systematic use by Herceg-Bosna/HVO forces of Bosnian Muslim detainees for unlawful forced labour; by promoting, instigating, encouraging, condoning the commission of crimes against Bosnian Muslims by failing to report and/or investigate crimes and/or by failing to punish or discipline subordinates and others responsible. And finally, by engaging in, encouraging, facilitating, or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. supporting efforts to deny, conceal, and/or minimise crimes committed by the Herceg-Bosna/HVO authorities and forces against Bosnian Muslims or other non-Croats. In paragraph 39 of the indictment, it is set out in what kind of criminal activities you were engaged in the view of the Prosecutor as a part of and in the course of the actions described otherwise in the indictment, including ethnic cleansing. And the Prosecutor confronts you with the following activities: With the instigation and fomentation of political, ethnic or religious strife, division and hatred: By speeches, propaganda, and false information, the Herceg-Bosna/HVO authorities created, instigated, and supported a charged anti-Muslim atmosphere, promoted ethnic division, and fostered religious mistrust; by the use of force, intimidation, and terror: Herceg-Bosna/HVO authorities and military and police units used force and the threat of force to dominate, suppress, and persecute Bosnian Muslims. In the course of mass arrests and evictions, Bosnian Muslims were killed, severely injured, sexually assaulted, robbed of their property, and otherwise abused. Under (c), it says that you engaged in appropriation and destruction of property, that Bosnian Muslims were to abandon their homes, and that money, cars, and personal property were often taken or looted. Paragraph 39 further mentions detention and imprisonment, that a system of ill-treatment was established, supported, and operated involving a network of prisons, concentration camps, and other detention facilities; that not only men, but also women, children, and elderly were arrested and detained and imprisoned; that they were kept, at least many of them, in horrible conditions and deprived of basic human necessities; and that they suffered inhuman treatment and physical and psychological abuse. Paragraph 39 further mentions the forcible transfer and deportation, that the system of ill-treatment was established, supported, and operated to deport Bosnian Muslims to other countries or transfer them to parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina not claimed or controlled by Herceg-Bosna. Finally, paragraph 39 mentions forced labour, that many Bosnian Muslims were held by the HVO, and that they were forced to engage in physical labour, including digging trenches and retrieving bodies, often in combat and dangerous conditions, which resulted in many Bosnian Muslims, detainees, being killed or severely wounded. Some of them were used as human shields. These are central parts of these indictments. I will now briefly indicate to you what locations are specifically referred to in the indictment, giving further details of what happened in these locations; that is Prozor Municipality, Gornji Vakuf Municipality, Sovici and Doljani, Jablanica, Mostar Municipality, the Heliodrom camp, the Vojno camp, the Ljubuski Municipality and Detention Centre, Stolac Municipality, Capilinja Municipality, Dretelj district military prison, Gabela district military prison, and Vares Municipality. At the end of each section on each of these municipalities, it's always mentioned that all six of you are responsible for the crimes that are then described in legal terms. And you'll find in those paragraphs also a reference to the listing in part 6 indicating what crimes were committed in that localities, although not every and each type of crime was, according to the indictment, committed in each of these municipalities. There are, however, two exceptions to the fact that you're held responsible, all six of you, for the crimes committed in all of these municipalities. Mr. Pusic, you are not charged with events that allegedly took place in Prozor Municipality in October 1992; that is, on the 23rd of October when the Herceg-Bosna/HVO forces attacked Bosnian Muslims in Prozor town, which attack was followed by plunder, arson, and destruction of Bosnian Muslim home and other properties, rounding up Bosnian Muslims, and detaining them. You are therefore also not charged with what happened on the 24th of October, as the indictment says, and that is an attack on Paljike, 1 kilometre south of Prozor town, which attack included the killing of two civilians and the detention of Bosnian Muslims. But the charges against you include the events that happened in 1993 as described in the indictment. The second exception of you being held responsible by the Prosecutor, all six for the events in all the locations, is that you, Mr. Pusic, you are not charged with what happened in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993, and therefore you'll see that your name does not appear in paragraph 72 of the indictment where only five names are mentioned as being responsible for what happened in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. This is a general overview and a summary of the indictment. Of course, it's not detailed in legal terms. It's not detailed in factual terms. But it is a summary. If either the Defence or the Prosecution or any of the accused finds that my summary is incorrect or should be supplemented, I'd like to hear it now so that we could refer to the specific part of the indictment you find is not properly presented in my summary. Is there any need for correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Prosecution, there's no need for any addition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the Defence is remaining silent, and I see no signs of any objection from the accused. So I take it that I do not need to correct or supplement my summary. Since you indicated that all six accused wanted to enter a plea today and not at a later stage, I'd first, after having given the summary, again ask a question to all accused, although I'm aware that some of you have already answered that question. Mr. Prlic, do you understand the indictment brought against you? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour. I understand the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, same question for you. Do you understand the indictment? THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour. I understand the indictment fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, may I ask you the same question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully understood the indictment in the language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally for you, Mr. Pusic. And I add to it that you are not held responsible for the events in Prozor in October 1992 and that you're not charged at all with the events in January 1993 in Gornji Vakuf. Did you understand, including this specific element, the indictment brought against you? THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] I understand the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'd invite you to enter a plea on each of the counts. I will read them to you count by count, and then ask whether you plead guilty or not guilty on that specific count. Count 1, persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(h), 7(1), and 7(3). Mr. Prlic, how do you plead to count 1? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to plead to all counts of the indictment. I don't think it is necessary to enumerate all of them, at least as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will read them all out. But if all accused intend to plead in the same way to all counts, I could read them one by one, and then ask you at the end whether you -- what your plea is on each of the 26 counts brought against you. But then I need some confirmation that you'll have a similar plea on each count because otherwise it would not function. May I ask it in a different way. If any one of you wants to give different pleas, to enter different pleas on the various counts, I'd like to be informed. Since I do not receive any reaction, I take it that you want to plead -- to enter the same plea on each count. I'll then read them one by one. Count 1, I'll repeat it. Persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(h), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 2, murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(a), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 3, willful killing, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(a), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 4, rape, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(g), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 5, inhuman treatment, (sexual assault), a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(b), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 6, deportation, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(d), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 7, unlawful deportation of a civilian, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(g), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 8, inhumane acts (forcible transfer), a crime against Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(i), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 9, unlawful transfer of a civilian, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(g), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 10, imprisonment, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(e), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 11, unlawful confinement of a civilian, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(g), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 12, inhumane acts (conditions of confinement), a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(i), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 13, inhuman treatment (conditions of confinement), a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(b), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 14, cruel treatment (conditions of confinement), a violation of the laws and customs of war as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions, punishable under Statute Articles 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Count 15, inhumane acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Statute Articles 5(i), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 16, inhuman treatment, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(b), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 17, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions, punishable under Statute Article 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Count 18, unlawful labour, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Articles 40, 51, and 95 of Geneva Convention IV and Articles 49, 50, and 52 of Geneva Convention III, punishable under Statute Articles 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Count 19, extensive destruction of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(d), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 20, wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, or devastation not justified by military necessity, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Statute Article 3(b), 7(1), and 7(3). Destruction or willful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion or education as count 21, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under the Statute Articles 3(d), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 22, appropriation of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(d), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 23, plunder of public or private property, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Statute Articles 3(e), 7(1), and 7(3). Count 24, unlawful attack on civilians (Mostar), a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised under customary law, and Article 51 of Additional Protocol I and Article 13 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Article 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Coming to count 25, Mr. Scott, could you already clarify the reference to Article 3(d).

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour has a fine eye, and I think it would be correct to say that the (d) is an error, the sub (d), and it should simply read "Articles 3, 7(1), and 7(3)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. I take it this will get a follow up in writing, Mr. Scott. Count 25, unlawful infliction of terror on civilians (Mostar), a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised under customary law, and Article 51 of Additional Protocol I and Article 13 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Article 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Count 26, cruel treatment (Mostar siege), a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions and punishable under Statute Articles 3, 7(1), and 7(3). Mr. Prlic, would you please stand. How do you plead to each and every of the 26 counts just read out to you? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I am not guilty, and the plea is the same to all counts. I was not a master of war as I have been made out to be in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, this is the moment where you are invited to enter a plea, not to give further statements. I do understand that you plead not guilty on all 26 counts. Is that correct? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I wanted to answer briefly in order to avoid answering to every individual count. I merely want to say two or three words. I do not mean to be giving a speech, so if I may be allowed to say two or three words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a custom in this courtroom that if you want to address the Court on anything you're not asked for, you ask permission for that. And since you -- I do understand what you say now is a request for adding a few words, I'll consider it and I'll let you know whether I'll give an opportunity to you to address the Court. Then please be seated. Mr. Stojic, how do you plead to each and every count of the -- of the 26 counts I just read to you? THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand the not guilty plea to be valid for all 26 counts? THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty on any of the counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojic. Mr. Praljak, I invite to you enter a plea on each and every of the 26 counts I just read to you. Do you plead guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Not guilty on any of the 26 counts of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. Mr. Petkovic, do you plead guilty or not guilty on each and every of the 26 counts just read to you? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty on any of the counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Coric, may I invite you to enter a plea on each of the 26 counts just read to you. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I plead not guilty on any of the counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pusic, may I invite you to enter a plea on each and every of the counts, the 26 counts, just read to you. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my plea is not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pusic. Madam Registrar, it should be put on record that all six accused have entered a plea of not guilty on each of the 26 counts brought against them. Since you have now all arrived in the UN Detention Unit, I'd like to hear from you whether there are any observations to be made in respect of the detention circumstances; whether there are any complaints or is there anything this Court should know about your detention circumstances? I'll put a similar question to you in respect of your health situation, whether the Chamber should be informed about specific aspects of your health or your family circumstances. If there's any need to go into private session, that means that the public will not hear what you say, please inform me because for reasons of privacy, we could especially on these issues go into private session when needed and requested. May I first, in respect of both detention circumstances and in respect of health and family situation, invite you, Mr. Prlic, to say whatever you would like to say. The other issue will be left for a later moment. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Except for the fact that I do not believe I should be kept in detention, I have no objections to make to the conditions of detention itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And from your silence, may I take it that health and family situation doesn't require any specific attention. May I then put the same question to you, Mr. Stojic. THE ACCUSED STOJIC: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour. No comments about any health issues or as regards the conditions of my detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Praljak, same question, three aspects to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no objections in relation to my family situation, my health, or the conditions of my detention. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petkovic, any submissions to be made in respect of -- THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] I have no complaints about the conditions of detention, and may they not be changed. I have no other comments. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] [Realtime transcript read in error "Mr. Choric"] Your Honour, I am not exactly thrilled by the fact that I am being held in detention, but as for the conditions of my detention, I have no complaints, and I feel well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Coric, would you please wait until a question is asked to you, not because I would be offended if you tell me something, but now it appears on the transcript as if Mr. Petkovic was still speaking, because you followed him up without any question being put in between, and then the transcribers who are responsible for the transcripts will just continue to write down the words spoken. And I therefore at this moment, I have to correct for the transcript. Yes, I see that it now says "Mr. Coric," not as usual "the accused Coric" but page 42, line 5, it's Mr. Coric who is speaking. Then Mr. Pusic, the same question to you, detention circumstances, health, and family circumstances. THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] No complaints about the conditions of my detention, Your Honour, or my family situation. The only thing I wish to say, Your Honour, if I may be allowed to ask for your permission, I only found out about the indictment while I was bedridden in Ljubljana, in a hospital. As my Defence counsel has already informed you, I voluntarily gave myself up to the Tribunal. And what I would like to ask for is to be medically examined by a doctor at the detention facility so that the relevant medical documents could be prepared. I have already sent some of my medical documents to the Tribunal when -- and I delivered some when I arrived in the prison unit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you one question. Have you already been seen by a doctor in the Detention Unit? THE ACCUSED PUSIC: [Interpretation] Yes, but it was a general practitioner, and I explained what my condition was about. The general practitioner then said he would inform one of his colleagues, a specialist in neurology, but none of the doctors have shown up so far. I do require further medical assistance and care. I think it is plain for all to see that my condition is not very good, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will take care that the attention of the Registrar will be drawn to the fact that you have been -- that you underwent surgery recently, and that proper attention is given to your medical condition. Whether that means that a specialist would see you today or yesterday or the day after tomorrow is not in my hands at this moment. But I'll look at it that the specific attention of the Registrar will be drawn to your health condition. Then Mr. Prlic, you wanted to address the Court, and although it's not a custom in this Court that statements are given in relation to the plea you entered, if you would like to clarify very shortly without giving speeches, I'll allow you to do so. But please, be aware if you want to make an unsworn statement at trial, the Rules specifically provide for you to give an unsworn statement. I also have to warn you that whatever you say here, it's up to the Chamber finally what value, what evidentiary value it would be given. So I don't know whether you consulted with counsel when you requested to address me. That's one issue. And the second is if you want to address the Chamber, although the other Judges will read the transcript, it might be a better occasion to do so when all three Judges are there. But if you want to make a very short statement, I would say not more than 1 to 2 minutes, then I'll give you an opportunity to do so. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honour. All I was about to say were two or three words, or rather sentences. I want to say that I sympathise with Bosnia and Herzegovina and all the victims referred to in the indictment. I merely wish to point out that I believe this Tribunal will give me an opportunity to present the truth about my own involvement in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the truth itself will set me free and acquit me on all the counts of the indictment. I just wish to add yet again, to reiterate, that I plead not guilty on all counts of the indictment. It was my original intention to say as much as this, and I don't think that is too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will get an opportunity in due course to present your case and to bring to the attention to the Chamber whatever you deem useful, and I do understand that you again wanted to underline your not guilty plea on all 26 counts. All the items on my agenda, apart from one, have been addressed. The one item still there is that the Chamber has received a -- no, perhaps we first turn into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any issue one of the parties, either Defence or Prosecution, would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No issues to be raised by the Prosecution. Let me then put it in a negative way: Do I well understand that no one of the Defence counsel wants to raise an issue at this very moment? Yes. Then, this concludes this Initial Appearance. There's no need at this moment to set new dates, since all the accused have entered pleas on all counts. Therefore, we'll adjourn without any new dates set at this very moment.
